Send Close Pediatric Infections Share on Facebook Share on LinkedIn Share on X Email Article Copy Article Url Print OCTOBER 23, 2026 IDWeek 2026 RSV-B Lineage Emerges as Standout in Severe Pediatric Disease By Anna Tsioulias Young children infected with certain respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) subgroup B lineages experienced greater disease severity than those infected with RSV-A, according to a study presented at IDWeek 2026, in Washington, D.C. Source: Adobe. The biggest potential culprit? RSV-B lineage B.D.E.1. Related Content RSV Vaccination Shows Effectiveness at Year 3 A new study has found that vaccination against respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) remains effective three years ... This Year’s U.S. Measles Cases Soar Beyond 4,000 The United States has identified 4,080 confirmed measles cases in 2026, as of CDC data updated on Oct. 8. Starting HPV Vaccine at Age 9 or 10 Raises Series Completion by 13 Starting the HPV vaccine series younger substantially increased the share of children who began and finished the ... The findings shed new light on a longstanding debate regarding the relative virulence of RSV antigenic subgroups. Although both RSV-A and RSV-B are established players in severe pediatric respiratory disease, prior studies have yielded conflicting results on whether differences in viral glycoproteins, including the fusion (F) and attachment (G) proteins, influence clinical severity. “We actually initially thought RSV-A was more pathogenic than RSV-B,” explained Kim El Haddad, MD, a pediatric infectious diseases physician at MedStar Georgetown University Hospital, in Washington, D.C. “These new findings help clarify with very statistically significant results that the lineage B was associated with worse outcomes, although the fact that this study had more RSV-B than RSV-A cases (216 vs. 129) might affect precision.” In a prospective study spanning seven respiratory seasons (2015-2021), investigators at St. Jude Children’s Research Hospital, in Memphis, Tennessee, collected nasal swabs from 345 previously healthy children younger than 2 years of age: 22% with mild (outpatient) and 78% with moderate to severe (inpatient) RSV infection. After whole-genome sequencing, significant differences emerged across six RSV lineages with regard to disease severity scores (P=0.01), pediatric ICU admissions (P<0.0001), duration of oxygen supplementation (P=0.04), oxygen delivery methods (P<0.0001), and hospital length of stay (P=0.03). B.D.E.1 (n=61) was associated with particularly severe clinical outcomes, with nearly three-fourths of infected children requiring PICU admission. However, Dr. El Haddad, who was not involved with the research, noted that the changing distribution of RSV lineages across respiratory seasons could complicate interpretation, especially considering disruptions in viral circulation during the COVID-19 pandemic. “During peak COVID times, isolation measures created what we call an immunity debt, as many children were not exposed to RSV,” Dr. El Haddad told Infectious Disease Special Edition. “When restrictions eased in 2021, we saw a surge in B.D.E.1 infections. I wonder whether this lack of previous exposure contributed to a stronger inflammatory response with elevated cytokine levels and ultimately more severe disease. “I would also be interested in knowing whether viral loads differed between RSV-A and RSV-B infections, as reflected by cycle threshold values. A higher viral burden could contribute to both the more pronounced inflammatory response and greater disease severity observed with certain RSV-B lineages.” Looking beyond differences in clinical severity, the investigators uncovered distinct genomic and inflammatory profiles among RSV subgroups. More specifically, RSV-B showed greater sequence variability across F, G, and M2-2 proteins, raising questions about potential implications for RSV immunoprophylaxis. Dr. El Haddad noted that nirsevimab (Beyfortus, Sanofi/AstraZeneca) and clesrovimab (Enflonsia, Merck) target the F protein, but whether the observed genetic variation influences monoclonal antibody effectiveness remains unknown; however, she considered a clinically meaningful impact unlikely. RSV-B infections were also linked with a more pronounced mucosal inflammatory response, with age-adjusted analyses identifying 22 cytokines at significantly higher concentrations than in RSV-A infections (P<0.01). These cytokines formed two distinct clusters: one involving innate immune activation and interleukin-1 signaling, the other with chemotaxis and cellular stress pathways. Of importance, previous RSV exposure and the associated immune response could potentially affect cytokine profiles and disease severity during subsequent infections, according to Dr. El Haddad. “As the authors didn’t mention it, I am interested to know whether any children had prior RSV infections. If prior infection was not accounted for, it could represent a potential confounder.” Dr. El Haddad reported no relevant financial disclosures.
